newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian king fears kidnapped Briton is dead.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian king fears kidnapped Briton is dead.

text.p: Cambodia's King Norodom Sihanouk believes Khmer Rouge guerrillas probably killed a British mine clearance expert abducted more than one year ago, according to a palace bulletin released on Monday.

"The respected Mr. (Christopher) Howes has been killed by the Khmer Rouge...It's more than likely," Sihanouk wrote by hand next to a clipping of an April 29 newspaper article about payment of a $120,000 ransom by the Briton's employees.

The British-based Mines Advisory Group (MAG) on November 18 gave the money to a Cambodian who said he could get Howes out of the northern Khmer Rouge base of Anlong Veng. He never showed up and $40,000 was returned to the humanitarian agency in February.
Military officials believe Howes and his interpreter Houn Hourth were taken to a base after their abduction by armed men in the northwest province of Siem Reap on March 26 last year.

"It's unfortunate to give US$120,000 to KR (Khmer Rouge) assassins to try to free poor Mr. Howes, whom the KR would never release," Sihanouk wrote in the bulletin, a collection of commentaries, letters, interviews and press articles.

The British government, which advises against ransom payments in kidnap cases, says it has no concrete information to indicate whether Howes is dead or alive. Scotland Yard detectives continue work on the case out of Siem Reap on a rotation basis.

Hopes were briefly raised last year when a top Cambodian general said Howes, Houn Hourth and a group of Khmer Rouge defectors had escaped from Anlong Veng and were headed for government lines. They never showed up.
Khieu Samphan, nominal leader of the Maoist-inspired group, has denied any knowledge of the whereabouts of Howes.
The Khmer Rouge, whose 1975-79 rule left more than one million people dead, signed a U.N.-brokered peace pact with rival factions in 1991.
They later reneged on the pact and have since fought the uneasy coalition government formed after U.N.-run general elections in 1993.
But the guerrilla movement, blamed for the abductions and murders of at least seven Westerners since 1993, began falling apart last year, with thousands of rebels defecting to the government.
Officials say less than 2,000 hardliners based around Anlong Veng are still holding out against peace.
